new_statements.quote: Apparently phonemic long vowels are so rare elsewhere as to be treated with suspicion, although they are currently written in a few words. Note, however, that non-phonemic lengthening of the stressed vowel of disyllabic words is a feature of Wanyi (hence the spelling Waanyi). [p. 427] ... one is the fact that nanda, as a demonstrative, is not normally as strongly stressed as a noun like banda, and so the retroflexion is not so obvious. [...] banda, initial bilabial stop, followed by a vowel [...] then the retroflexed apical nasal and stop, and finally an unstressed low central vowel. [p. 428]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened (extracted text, PDF pages 3-4 = printed pp. 427-428, running heads "Wanyi and Garrwa comparative data 427" / "428 Gavan Breen"). All three spliced fragments of the reported quote are present verbatim: p. 427 (§2 Phonology, first paragraph) "Apparently phonemic long vowels are so rare elsewhere as to be treated with suspicion, although they are currently written in a few words. Note, however, that non-phonemic lengthening of the stressed vowel of disyllabic words is a feature of Wanyi (hence the spelling Waanyi)."; p. 428 "one is the fact that nanda, as a demonstrative, is not normally as strongly stressed as a noun like banda, and so the retroflexion is not so obvious." and "ba…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No explicit rule is stated in any accessible source. Breen's phonology notes presuppose that the stressed vowel of a disyllable is the first one (the stressed, non-phonemically lengthened /a/ of Wanyi gives the spelling 'Waanyi'; banda 'camp' ends in an unstressed vowel), and Laughren 2016:189 speaks of extra-strong stress 'on its initial syllable' for trisyllabic verbs (yunngumbu, burrbijbi). Together these point to word-initial primary stress, the pattern Furby 1974:11 states explicitly for the sister language Garrwa ('primary stress.. is always on the first syllable of the phonological word'). Provisional reading: fixed initial stress; inferred, not asserted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Wanyi. For sister-language Garrwa, Furby 1974:11: secondary stress on the penultimate syllable of words of four or more syllables, tertiary on alternate syllables before it, never on the second syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Breen 2003:428 notes that demonstratives (nanda) are 'not normally as strongly stressed' as nouns — a word-class/phrasal prominence difference, not a positional exception. Laughren 2016:189 describes emphatic extra-strong stress on a verb's initial syllable in post-enclitic position (phrase-level prominence).
new_statements.domain_note: Breen's remarks concern citation-form words (disyllabic nouns, demonstratives) from his 1970s fieldwork with Ivy George and other Wanyi speakers; Laughren's concerns verbs in clause context (Roy Seccin, 2000s fieldwork). Phrase-level: enclitic subject pronouns attach to the clause-initial word.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen 2003 describes Wanyi (his spelling; = Waanyi, wany1247, ISO wny) from his 1970s fieldwork with Ivy George (Riversleigh) and others; Laughren's data are from Roy Seccin (Borroloola area, also a Garrwa speaker). Breen treats Wanyi as a close relative or distant dialect of Garrwa (83% Eastern-Western Garrwa cognacy vs 66% Eastern Garrwa-Wanyi). The explicit stress rule in Furby 1974 is for Western Garrwa (garr1259, ISO wrk), a different catalog language.

sources.quote: Apparently phonemic long vowels are so rare elsewhere as to be treated with suspicion, although they are currently written in a few words. Note, however, that non-phonemic lengthening of the stressed vowel of disyllabic words is a feature of Wanyi (hence the spelling Waanyi). [p. 427] ... one is the fact that nanda, as a demonstrative, is not normally as strongly stressed as a noun like banda, and so the retroflexion is not so obvious. [...] banda, initial bilabial stop, followed by a vowel [...] then the retroflexed apical nasal and stop, and finally an unstressed low central vowel. [p. 428]
sources.note: §2 Phonology (pp. 427-429) has no stress rule as such, but states that 'non-phonemic lengthening of the stressed vowel of disyllabic words is a feature of Wanyi (hence the spelling Waanyi)' (p. 427), i.e. the first vowel of a disyllable is the stressed one; p. 428 describes banda 'camp' as ending in 'an unstressed low central vowel' and says the demonstrative nanda 'is not normally as strongly stressed as a noun like banda'. Implicitly initial stress; nothing on secondary stress or longer words.
